screens.title: Use Cases and Best Practices for Site-to-Site VPN
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore practical use cases and operational best practices for AWS Site-to-Site VPN. We'll cover the scenarios where VPN is the right choice, how it contrasts with Direct Connect, and how to design resilient, secure, and cost-aware hybrid connectivity. You will learn concrete patterns such as using VPN for development and testing, temporary projects, small branch offices, disaster recovery, and as a backup to Direct Connect. We will also unpack architecture patterns that improve availability — dual tunnels, multiple customer gateways, diverse ISPs, and Transit Gateway attachments — and walk through security controls like strong pre-shared keys, up-to-date IPsec parameters, and strict firewall rules. Finally, we'll review cost components and optimizations such as monitoring data transfer, consolidating traffic with Transit Gateway, and when to evaluate Direct Connect for high-volume use. By the end you'll be able to justify when to use VPN, design a failover plan, and apply security and cost best practices that protect operations. Think about one connection you manage now and how a VPN backup could improve its reliability.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Use Cases and Best Practices for Site-to-Site VPN
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Use Cases and Best Practices

Understand when Site-to-Site VPN is right, how to make it resilient and secure, and how to control costs in hybrid architectures.

Duration: ~10 min presentation
In this lesson
  • Identify practical VPN use cases: dev/test, DR, branch offices, temporary links.
  • Contrast VPN and Direct Connect for workload fit.
  • Design highly available VPN architectures and security controls.
Why it matters

Picking the right hybrid connectivity protects performance, cost, and continuity. VPN provides fast, encrypted options that can be hardened for production when designed carefully.

Explore Key Topics
Core patterns and decisions you will use to design reliable hybrid networks.
VPN Use Cases
Dev/test, DR, small branches, temporary links.
HA Patterns
Dual tunnels, multiple CGWs, Transit Gateway attachments.
Security & Cost
Strong PSKs, updated crypto, monitor tunnel data out.
Visual Summary
Overview
Primary vs Backup Pattern
Use Direct Connect as primary for consistent performance and Site-to-Site VPN as encrypted failover over the internet.
Transit Gateway Fit
Centralize multiple VPNs and VPCs for scalable hub-and-spoke topologies.
Watchouts
Avoid overlapping IPs and test changes in staging before production.
Getting Started
Think about one service that needs predictable performance. Would you use Direct Connect or VPN? Why?
Tip: small branches and short-lived projects favor VPN; mission-critical, high-throughput workloads favor Direct Connect.

screens.title: Primary Use Cases for Site-to-Site VPN
screens.narratorSegment: Site-to-Site VPN is an encrypted network tunnel between your on-premises network and AWS. Its core strengths are rapid deployment, modest cost, and use of existing internet connectivity. A clear example is development and testing environments: teams often need quick, secure access to cloud resources without provisioning a physical circuit. VPN lets them spin up access in minutes to hours, which speeds development cycles. Another common use is disaster recovery. VPN provides a cost-effective path to replicate data or bring up a recovery environment in AWS; while Direct Connect may be preferred for primary DR because of predictable performance, VPN is an effective backup or for less critical recovery tasks. Small branch offices also benefit from VPN because setting up dedicated lines for each location can be cost-prohibitive. Temporary connectivity needs — migrations, proofs of concept, or short-term projects — align well with VPN as well. A common misconception is that VPN is always too slow; while internet performance can vary, VPNs are suitable for moderate bandwidth needs and can be hardened for many production uses. Takeaway: use VPN when you need secure, quick, and cost-effective hybrid connectivity or as a backup for more robust primary links. How would you justify VPN for a small branch with limited IT budget?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Site-to-Site VPN is an encrypted hybrid link best for dev/test, DR backups, small branch offices, and temporary or backup connectivity when dedicated circuits aren't justified.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Primary Use Cases
Core Concept

Situations that favor Site-to-Site VPN

Quickly establish encrypted connectivity for scenarios where dedicated private circuits are unnecessary or impractical.

Development & Testing
Example: dev teams need secure access to cloud resources during feature testing without a long procurement cycle.
Disaster Recovery (Backup)
Example: replicate backups to AWS or spin up a recovery site; VPN acts as a cost-effective replication path or fallback.
Small Branch Offices & Temporary Links
Example: branch offices or short-term migrations where dedicated circuits are not justified.
Supporting Details
  • VPN is encrypted by default and leverages your existing internet link.
  • Typical throughput per tunnel is limited; aggregate multiple tunnels for higher bandwidth.
  • Deployment is fast—minutes to hours—compared to dedicated circuits.
  • Best practice: use VPN as a backup to Direct Connect for critical workloads.
Example
A dev team sets up a VPN to access test databases in a VPC while the production Direct Connect is reserved for the live database.
Key Takeaway
Use VPN for fast, encrypted connectivity when performance needs are moderate or as a backup to dedicated links.

screens.title: Site-to-Site VPN vs. Direct Connect
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing AWS Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect helps you choose the right primary and backup links. Site-to-Site VPN is quick to deploy, cost-effective, and encrypted by default. It relies on the public internet, so latency, jitter, and throughput can vary; each VPN tunnel has a maximum throughput typically around 1.25 Gbps, and you can aggregate traffic across tunnels or multiple connections. Direct Connect provides a dedicated private circuit with consistent performance, lower latency, and much higher throughput—up to tens of gigabits—making it ideal for high-volume, latency-sensitive, or compliance-driven workloads. However, Direct Connect takes longer to provision and has higher fixed costs like port fees and data transfer out. A common misconception is to assume VPN is only for non-production use; in many architectures VPN is suitable for production where moderate bandwidth and encryption are sufficient. A recommended hybrid approach is Direct Connect as the primary high-performance link and Site-to-Site VPN as encrypted failover. Example: a latency-sensitive database migration would use Direct Connect as primary and VPN as the backup to maintain continuity during circuit outages. What trade-offs in your environment would drive you to choose Direct Connect first?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › VPN vs Direct Connect
Comparison

Site-to-Site VPN

  • Pros: fast deployment, pay-as-you-go, encrypted by default, uses existing internet link.
  • Cons: variable internet performance, throughput limits per tunnel, requires on-prem VPN device.
  • Best for: moderate bandwidth, rapid deployment, backups, small branches, dev/test.
Concrete Example
A short-term migration uses VPN to securely move test traffic while a Direct Connect circuit is provisioned for production.
Comparison

AWS Direct Connect

  • Pros: dedicated private connection, consistent performance, lower latency, high throughput.
  • Cons: longer provisioning time, higher cost, requires colocation at a Direct Connect location.
  • Best for: high bandwidth, low latency, large data transfers, strict compliance.
Concrete Example
A production database replication stream uses Direct Connect for predictable latency and throughput.
Hybrid Best Practice
Use Direct Connect as primary for mission-critical performance and Site-to-Site VPN as encrypted failover to ensure business continuity when the primary circuit fails.

screens.title: Designing for High Availability and Resiliency
screens.narratorSegment: High availability for Site-to-Site VPN is achieved by layering redundancy across tunnels, devices, ISPs, and AWS connectivity. Start with the built-in dual tunnels that AWS provides for each VPN connection; configure both tunnels on your on-premises device and use BGP so the routing can fail over automatically. For higher resilience, create multiple VPN connections to distinct Customer Gateways — that is, use different VPN devices or devices in separate data centers. This protects against single-device failures. Also consider connecting each Customer Gateway to a different ISP so you aren't dependent on one provider. If your environment has many VPCs or on-premises sites, use Transit Gateway as a hub to centralize attachments; Transit Gateway allows you to attach multiple VPNs and simplifies routing across the network. A practical misconception is assuming a single dual-tunnel VPN is sufficient for mission-critical workloads; while dual tunnels protect against a tunnel failure, they don't protect against on-prem device or ISP outages. Example: configure two VPN connections, each to a separate CGW with different ISPs, and attach them to a Transit Gateway so traffic can reroute if one path fails. Key question: what single point of failure remains in your design and how would you remove it?

keyIdea.text: Build resilience with dual tunnels, multiple VPN connections to different CGWs, diverse ISPs, and centralize with Transit Gateway for scalable failover.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Designing HA
Process Flow

Steps to build resilient VPNs

  1. Enable both built-in tunnels and configure BGP to allow automatic failover between tunnels.
  2. Create multiple VPN connections to separate Customer Gateways or devices to avoid single-device failure.
  3. Use diverse ISPs for those CGWs to mitigate provider outages.
  4. Attach multiple VPNs to a Transit Gateway for scalable hub-and-spoke routing and centralized management.
  5. Test failover and maintain monitoring so you detect and respond to outages quickly.
Design Cards
Dual Tunnels
Always configure both tunnels and enable BGP for automatic path selection.
Multiple CGWs
Use separate VPN devices or datacenters to protect against device-level failure.
Transit Gateway
Centralize and scale many VPN attachments; simplifies any-to-any connectivity for many VPCs.
Key Takeaway
Resilience requires layered redundancy: tunnel, device, ISP, and cloud-side architecture.

screens.title: Security Best Practices for Site-to-Site VPN
screens.narratorSegment: Security for Site-to-Site VPN begins with strong cryptography and careful operational controls. Use long, randomly generated pre-shared keys for each tunnel and never reuse keys across connections. Configure IPsec parameters to use strong algorithms such as AES-256 and SHA256 and prefer strong Diffie-Hellman groups when supported by both ends. These settings reduce the risk of brute force and cryptographic weaknesses. Implement strict firewall rules on both sides — on-premises firewalls and AWS Security Groups or Network ACLs — to allow only the necessary traffic and follow the principle of least privilege. Limit administrative access to VPN devices and AWS resources with fine-grained IAM roles. Perform regular audits of VPN configurations, logs, and cryptographic parameters so standards remain current as algorithms evolve. A common misconception is that default settings are sufficient; defaults may be acceptable, but you must verify parameters and rotate keys periodically. Example: rotate pre-shared keys on a maintenance schedule and verify tunnels re-establish correctly. Takeaway: combine strong algorithms, rigorous access controls, and periodic audits to maintain a secure hybrid link. What audit steps will you schedule quarterly for your VPNs?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Security Best Practices
Security

Hardening Site-to-Site VPN

  • Use long, unique pre-shared keys per tunnel and rotate them on a schedule.
  • Configure strong IPsec parameters: AES-256, SHA256, and a strong Diffie-Hellman group supported by both ends.
  • Apply strict firewall rules and security groups that follow least privilege principle.
  • Restrict administrative access with IAM roles and limit who can manage VPN resources and CGWs.
  • Audit configurations and logs periodically to ensure cryptography and rules remain up to date.
Practical Controls
PSK Hygiene
Generate unique keys and store them securely; avoid reuse across tunnels.
Crypto Parameters
Prefer AES-256 and SHA256; review parameters as standards evolve.
Firewall Rules
Allow only necessary ports and source/destination ranges across both sides.
Audits
Schedule periodic checks of configs, logs, and key rotation status.
Example
Rotate PSKs during a maintenance window and validate both tunnels re-establish with BGP before returning to production.

screens.title: Cost Components and Optimization Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Cost for Site-to-Site VPN is driven primarily by two components: the VPN connection hourly charge and Data Transfer Out from AWS to your on-premises network. Data transferred into AWS over VPN is generally free, while data leaving AWS is billed at standard regional DTO rates. A first step in cost control is monitoring. Use CloudWatch metrics such as TunnelDataOut to identify where traffic is concentrated and which applications generate the most egress. One optimization is traffic consolidation: if multiple small VPNs terminate to the same on-premises location, consider consolidating them or centralizing with Transit Gateway to reduce the number of hourly connections. If DTO over VPN is consistently large, perform a cost analysis — it may be more cost-effective to provision Direct Connect, which often has lower per-GB DTO rates for high-volume transfers despite higher fixed costs. Another practical optimization is to disable or delete unused VPN connections to stop hourly charges. A common misconception is to ignore DTO because hourly costs seem small; high sustained egress can dominate monthly bills. Example: track TunnelDataOut across connections for a month to find a candidate for Direct Connect evaluation. What metric would you monitor this week to find cost savings?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Cost & Optimization
Cost Considerations

Primary cost drivers

  • VPN Connection Hour: hourly charge for each active VPN connection.
  • Data Transfer Out: charges for data leaving AWS over the VPN; monitor closely.
  • Inbound data to AWS over VPN is generally free.
Monitoring & Example
Use CloudWatch TunnelDataOut to identify high-traffic flows; if a single VPN shows sustained high DTO, model Direct Connect costs versus VPN DTO charges.
Optimization Tips
Monitor Data
Track TunnelDataOut and identify high-cost flows.
Consolidate Traffic
Use Transit Gateway to centralize VPNs and reduce per-connection overhead.
Evaluate Direct Connect
If DTO is consistently high, Direct Connect can be more economical despite higher fixed costs.
Disable Unused VPNs
Delete inactive connections to stop hourly charges.
Key Takeaway
Small hourly costs can compound; monitor DTO and consolidate or upgrade when volume justifies it.

screens.title: Transit Gateway and Centralized VPN Topologies
screens.narratorSegment: Transit Gateway is a scalable hub for connecting multiple VPCs and on-premises networks. When you have many VPN connections or several VPCs, attaching VPNs to a Transit Gateway simplifies routing and reduces complexity. Transit Gateway enables any-to-any routing between attached VPCs and on-premises networks, which makes it easier to manage many site connections without dozens of pairwise links. A practical example is consolidating multiple small branch VPNs that previously terminated to individual VGWs: attach those VPNs to a Transit Gateway and centralize routing policies. This can also be combined with Direct Connect by attaching a Direct Connect gateway to the Transit Gateway, enabling consistent routing across both private circuits and VPN backups. A misconception is that Transit Gateway always increases cost savings; while it simplifies operations and can reduce the number of VPNs, Transit Gateway has its own costs and should be chosen when operational simplicity and scale justify it. Takeaway: use Transit Gateway when you need scalable, centralized routing for many VPNs and VPCs and consider cost and traffic patterns before consolidating. How would you evaluate whether Transit Gateway makes sense for your network?

keyIdea.title: Transit Gateway fit
keyIdea.text: Transit Gateway centralizes routing and scales multiple VPN and VPC attachments, simplifying management for complex hybrid topologies.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Transit Gateway
Architecture

When to centralize with Transit Gateway

Transit Gateway provides a central hub for many VPNs and VPCs, enabling simplified routing and any-to-any connectivity where appropriate.

Benefits
Simpler routing, scalable attachments, consistent management of many connections.
Considerations
Transit Gateway has costs; evaluate traffic patterns to ensure benefits outweigh expenses.
Quick Scenario
If you manage dozens of small branch VPNs, attach them to a Transit Gateway to avoid complex peering and per-VPC routing tables. Combine with Direct Connect gateway for consistent private connectivity.
Key Takeaway
Transit Gateway simplifies scale and routing, but weigh costs and traffic before consolidating.

screens.title: BGP, Dual Tunnels, and Automatic Failover
screens.narratorSegment: BGP is the recommended routing mechanism for Site-to-Site VPN because it supports dynamic route exchange and automatic failover between tunnels. AWS provides two tunnels per VPN connection. When you configure BGP on both sides, route advertisements and path attributes allow traffic to switch when a tunnel or path becomes unavailable. A concrete example: if the primary tunnel loses connectivity, BGP withdraws the affected routes and your on-premises device will select the alternate path automatically, minimizing downtime. BGP also lets you influence route preference through attributes such as local preference or AS path length when you have multiple connections including Direct Connect. A common misconception is to rely on static routes only; static routing requires manual changes for failover and increases recovery time. For mission-critical systems, pair BGP with the multi-layer redundancy patterns we discussed — multiple CGWs and diverse ISPs — so routing failover handles tunnel outages while device or ISP failures are covered by additional connections. Takeaway: use BGP with dual tunnels for automatic route failover and plan for cross-device and ISP diversity to address broader outages. What BGP attribute would you adjust to prefer Direct Connect over VPN under normal conditions?

narration.text: BGP is the recommended routing mechanism for Site-to-Site VPN because it supports dynamic route exchange and automatic failover between tunnels. AWS provides two tunnels per VPN connection. When you configure BGP on both sides, route advertisements and path attributes allow traffic to switch when a tunnel or path becomes unavailable. A concrete example: if the primary tunnel loses connectivity, BGP withdraws the affected routes and your on-premises device will select the alternate path automatically, minimizing downtime. BGP also lets you influence route preference through attributes such as local preference or AS path length when you have multiple connections including Direct Connect. A common misconception is to rely on static routes only; static routing requires manual changes for failover and increases recovery time. For mission-critical systems, pair BGP with the multi-layer redundancy patterns we discussed — multiple CGWs and diverse ISPs — so routing failover handles tunnel outages while device or ISP failures are covered by additional connections. Takeaway: use BGP with dual tunnels for automatic route failover and plan for cross-device and ISP diversity to address broader outages. What BGP attribute would you adjust to prefer Direct Connect over VPN under normal conditions?

keyIdea.text: Use BGP with dual tunnels to enable automatic route withdrawal and failover; adjust BGP attributes to prefer Direct Connect over VPN when needed.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › BGP & Failover
Process

BGP enables automatic route failover

With BGP, AWS and your on-premises router exchange routes. If a tunnel fails, BGP withdraws routes so traffic moves to the remaining path without manual intervention.

  • Automatic withdrawal and re-advertisement of routes on failure.
  • Use BGP attributes to prefer Direct Connect under normal operation.
  • Combine BGP with dual tunnels, multiple CGWs, and diverse ISPs for full resilience.
Example Route Behavior
# Conceptual BGP flow
# Primary tunnel: preferred
advertise 172.31.0.0/16 via tunnel-0

# If tunnel-0 fails
withdraw 172.31.0.0/16
# Secondary tunnel now carries the route
advertise 172.31.0.0/16 via tunnel-1
Key Takeaway
BGP plus dual tunnels gives automatic route switching; static routes lack that agility and slow recovery.

screens.title: AWS and On-Prem Components for a Resilient Design
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing a resilient hybrid link requires planning both cloud-side and on-premises components. On the AWS side, you will use a Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) to terminate standard Site-to-Site VPNs directly to a VPC, or attach VPNs to a Transit Gateway when centralization is needed. For Direct Connect, a Direct Connect Gateway connects your physical circuit to one or more VGWs or Transit Gateways. On-premises, represent your physical device as a Customer Gateway in AWS and ensure you have at least two redundant routers or VPN devices if you aim for high availability. Use different ISPs where possible so a single ISP outage doesn't take down all paths. BGP must be configured on both sides for automatic routing and failover. Also plan firewall rules to allow only necessary traffic between the on-premises CIDR and VPC CIDR, and ensure no overlapping IP ranges exist between networks. A common operational oversight is insufficient on-prem redundancy; to prevent this, provision a second VPN device in a separate rack or datacenter and attach it to a different ISP. Takeaway: document each AWS and on-prem component required for your design and validate routing and firewall rules in staging before production deployment. AWS & On-prem building blocks

screens.title: Change Management, Testing, and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Operational discipline protects hybrid networks from avoidable outages. Follow change management for any production hybrid network change: document the change, test in a staging environment that mirrors production, schedule a maintenance window, and prepare a rollback plan. Testing should include verifying that both VPN tunnels come up with BGP and that failover behaves as expected. Regularly audit configurations and logs to detect drift or misconfiguration. A critical common mistake is overlapping IP address spaces between on-premises and VPCs; this causes routing failures and can be hard to debug. Always validate CIDR planning early in network design. Another pitfall is leaving unused VPN connections active; unused connections accrue hourly charges and increase attack surface. Finally, avoid weak pre-shared keys and outdated IPsec parameters. Example operational flow: submit a change ticket, deploy to staging, run failover tests, and then apply during the approved window with a rollback plan. Takeaway: planned, tested, and audited changes minimize risk and cost. Which operational control will you enforce first in your team? Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Change Management
Process

Safe operational practices

  1. Document the change and prepare a rollback plan.
  2. Test in a staging environment that mirrors production.
  3. Verify both tunnels establish and BGP failover behavior before deployment.
  4. Schedule an approved maintenance window and communicate impacts.
  5. Audit after the change and confirm monitoring is healthy.
Common Mistakes
Overlapping IPs, weak pre-shared keys, no redundancy for on-prem devices, and leaving unused VPNs active are frequent causes of outages and unnecessary cost.
Example
A team deployed a new VPC that overlapped with on-prem IPs and caused immediate routing failures; the lesson is to validate CIDRs early.
Key Takeaway
Follow disciplined change management, test failover, and avoid address overlaps to reduce risk.

screens.title: Design a Resilient Hybrid Connectivity Solution (Activity)
screens.narratorSegment: This activity guides you to design a resilient hybrid connectivity solution between an on-premises data center and an AWS VPC. Start by selecting your primary connectivity: for mission-critical and latency-sensitive applications, choose Direct Connect because it offers a dedicated circuit with predictable performance. For the backup, select Site-to-Site VPN to provide an encrypted failover over the public internet. Next, design redundancy: provision a Direct Connect connection and at least two VPN connections. Configure two Customer Gateways for VPNs on separate physical devices or locations and connect each to different ISPs to avoid a single ISP outage. Attach the VPNs and the Direct Connect gateway to a Transit Gateway if you have multiple VPCs or expect growth; this centralizes routing. Configure BGP on all connections so routes are exchanged dynamically and failover is automatic. Enforce security best practices: unique long PSKs for each tunnel, AES-256/SHA256 where supported, strict firewall rules permitting only necessary traffic, and IAM controls for VPN management. Finally, outline your monitoring and cost controls: watch TunnelDataOut, delete unused VPNs, and run a cost comparison of sustained DTO against Direct Connect monthly fees. Takeaway: a resilient hybrid design combines Direct Connect for primary performance and VPN for encrypted backup, with redundancy, BGP, and strong security. What will your primary and backup choices be for the scenario you just reviewed?

In this lesson we explore practical use cases and operational best practices for AWS Site-to-Site VPN. We'll cover the scenarios where VPN is the right choice, how it contrasts with Direct Connect, and how to design resilient, secure, and cost-aware hybrid connectivity. You will learn concrete patterns such as using VPN for development and testing, temporary projects, small branch offices, disaster recovery, and as a backup to Direct Connect. We will also unpack architecture patterns that improve availability — dual tunnels, multiple customer gateways, diverse ISPs, and Transit Gateway attachments — and walk through security controls like strong pre-shared keys, up-to-date IPsec parameters, and strict firewall rules. Finally, we'll review cost components and optimizations such as monitoring data transfer, consolidating traffic with Transit Gateway, and when to evaluate Direct Connect for high-volume use. By the end you'll be able to justify when to use VPN, design a failover plan, and apply security and cost best practices that protect operations. Think about one connection you manage now and how a VPN backup could improve its reliability.

These four objectives describe the core skills you'll gain from the chapter. First, you will evaluate appropriate use cases for Site-to-Site VPN by matching workload needs to VPN characteristics such as encryption, deployment speed, and bandwidth. For example, you'll learn why development and testing environments often use VPN instead of a dedicated line because of cost and setup time. Second, you will compare and contrast Site-to-Site VPN with Direct Connect so you can pick the right primary connection for a workload. We'll show the trade-offs in latency, throughput limits, provisioning time, and costs. Third, you'll design highly available and resilient VPN architectures using AWS features like dual tunnels, multiple customer gateways, and Transit Gateway attachments. You'll practice resilience patterns so services tolerate device and ISP failures. Fourth, you'll implement security best practices such as strong pre-shared keys, modern IPsec parameters, and strict firewall rules. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you recall the milestone and a verified competency note to mark your progress.

These four objectives extend your operational and design skills for Site-to-Site VPN. First, you will understand cost components for VPN, specifically the hourly VPN connection charge and data transfer out, and learn to monitor and control those costs. For example, you will practice using CloudWatch metrics like TunnelDataOut to find high-traffic flows. Second, you'll learn to consolidate traffic and use Transit Gateway to centralize multiple VPNs to reduce per-connection overhead and simplify routing. Third, you will configure BGP and take advantage of the built-in dual tunnels for automatic failover; we will explain route preference and how BGP enables seamless switchover. Fourth, you will adopt operational controls: change management, staging tests, and avoiding overlapping IP address ranges that can break connectivity. Each objective is framed as a practical skill you can demonstrate in a design review or template. By mastering these, you'll be able to recommend when to upgrade to Direct Connect and how to keep VPNs secure, resilient, and cost-effective.

Site-to-Site VPN is an encrypted network tunnel between your on-premises network and AWS. Its core strengths are rapid deployment, modest cost, and use of existing internet connectivity. A clear example is development and testing environments: teams often need quick, secure access to cloud resources without provisioning a physical circuit. VPN lets them spin up access in minutes to hours, which speeds development cycles. Another common use is disaster recovery. VPN provides a cost-effective path to replicate data or bring up a recovery environment in AWS; while Direct Connect may be preferred for primary DR because of predictable performance, VPN is an effective backup or for less critical recovery tasks. Small branch offices also benefit from VPN because setting up dedicated lines for each location can be cost-prohibitive. Temporary connectivity needs — migrations, proofs of concept, or short-term projects — align well with VPN as well. A common misconception is that VPN is always too slow; while internet performance can vary, VPNs are suitable for moderate bandwidth needs and can be hardened for many production uses. Takeaway: use VPN when you need secure, quick, and cost-effective hybrid connectivity or as a backup for more robust primary links. How would you justify VPN for a small branch with limited IT budget?

Comparing AWS Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect helps you choose the right primary and backup links. Site-to-Site VPN is quick to deploy, cost-effective, and encrypted by default. It relies on the public internet, so latency, jitter, and throughput can vary; each VPN tunnel has a maximum throughput typically around 1.25 Gbps, and you can aggregate traffic across tunnels or multiple connections. Direct Connect provides a dedicated private circuit with consistent performance, lower latency, and much higher throughput—up to tens of gigabits—making it ideal for high-volume, latency-sensitive, or compliance-driven workloads. However, Direct Connect takes longer to provision and has higher fixed costs like port fees and data transfer out. A common misconception is to assume VPN is only for non-production use; in many architectures VPN is suitable for production where moderate bandwidth and encryption are sufficient. A recommended hybrid approach is Direct Connect as the primary high-performance link and Site-to-Site VPN as encrypted failover. Example: a latency-sensitive database migration would use Direct Connect as primary and VPN as the backup to maintain continuity during circuit outages. What trade-offs in your environment would drive you to choose Direct Connect first?

High availability for Site-to-Site VPN is achieved by layering redundancy across tunnels, devices, ISPs, and AWS connectivity. Start with the built-in dual tunnels that AWS provides for each VPN connection; configure both tunnels on your on-premises device and use BGP so the routing can fail over automatically. For higher resilience, create multiple VPN connections to distinct Customer Gateways — that is, use different VPN devices or devices in separate data centers. This protects against single-device failures. Also consider connecting each Customer Gateway to a different ISP so you aren't dependent on one provider. If your environment has many VPCs or on-premises sites, use Transit Gateway as a hub to centralize attachments; Transit Gateway allows you to attach multiple VPNs and simplifies routing across the network. A practical misconception is assuming a single dual-tunnel VPN is sufficient for mission-critical workloads; while dual tunnels protect against a tunnel failure, they don't protect against on-prem device or ISP outages. Example: configure two VPN connections, each to a separate CGW with different ISPs, and attach them to a Transit Gateway so traffic can reroute if one path fails. Key question: what single point of failure remains in your design and how would you remove it?

Security for Site-to-Site VPN begins with strong cryptography and careful operational controls. Use long, randomly generated pre-shared keys for each tunnel and never reuse keys across connections. Configure IPsec parameters to use strong algorithms such as AES-256 and SHA256 and prefer strong Diffie-Hellman groups when supported by both ends. These settings reduce the risk of brute force and cryptographic weaknesses. Implement strict firewall rules on both sides — on-premises firewalls and AWS Security Groups or Network ACLs — to allow only the necessary traffic and follow the principle of least privilege. Limit administrative access to VPN devices and AWS resources with fine-grained IAM roles. Perform regular audits of VPN configurations, logs, and cryptographic parameters so standards remain current as algorithms evolve. A common misconception is that default settings are sufficient; defaults may be acceptable, but you must verify parameters and rotate keys periodically. Example: rotate pre-shared keys on a maintenance schedule and verify tunnels re-establish correctly. Takeaway: combine strong algorithms, rigorous access controls, and periodic audits to maintain a secure hybrid link. What audit steps will you schedule quarterly for your VPNs?

Cost for Site-to-Site VPN is driven primarily by two components: the VPN connection hourly charge and Data Transfer Out from AWS to your on-premises network. Data transferred into AWS over VPN is generally free, while data leaving AWS is billed at standard regional DTO rates. A first step in cost control is monitoring. Use CloudWatch metrics such as TunnelDataOut to identify where traffic is concentrated and which applications generate the most egress. One optimization is traffic consolidation: if multiple small VPNs terminate to the same on-premises location, consider consolidating them or centralizing with Transit Gateway to reduce the number of hourly connections. If DTO over VPN is consistently large, perform a cost analysis — it may be more cost-effective to provision Direct Connect, which often has lower per-GB DTO rates for high-volume transfers despite higher fixed costs. Another practical optimization is to disable or delete unused VPN connections to stop hourly charges. A common misconception is to ignore DTO because hourly costs seem small; high sustained egress can dominate monthly bills. Example: track TunnelDataOut across connections for a month to find a candidate for Direct Connect evaluation. What metric would you monitor this week to find cost savings?

Transit Gateway is a scalable hub for connecting multiple VPCs and on-premises networks. When you have many VPN connections or several VPCs, attaching VPNs to a Transit Gateway simplifies routing and reduces complexity. Transit Gateway enables any-to-any routing between attached VPCs and on-premises networks, which makes it easier to manage many site connections without dozens of pairwise links. A practical example is consolidating multiple small branch VPNs that previously terminated to individual VGWs: attach those VPNs to a Transit Gateway and centralize routing policies. This can also be combined with Direct Connect by attaching a Direct Connect gateway to the Transit Gateway, enabling consistent routing across both private circuits and VPN backups. A misconception is that Transit Gateway always increases cost savings; while it simplifies operations and can reduce the number of VPNs, Transit Gateway has its own costs and should be chosen when operational simplicity and scale justify it. Takeaway: use Transit Gateway when you need scalable, centralized routing for many VPNs and VPCs and consider cost and traffic patterns before consolidating.
